# Introduction to C: types, pointers and arrays {#sec-ch-c-intro}

> *"C is quirky, flawed, and an enormous success."* — Dennis Ritchie
> [@ritchie1993].

```{python}
from cppbook import run, show, sh, sanitizer_summary
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- write, compile and run a C program, and print values with `printf` and its
  format specifiers;
- choose among C's **integer types**, state their guaranteed ranges, use the
  fixed-width types of `<stdint.h>`, and **prove** that unsigned arithmetic is
  arithmetic modulo $2^n$;
- explain **undefined behaviour**, show how signed overflow lets the optimiser
  produce surprising code, and predict the **usual arithmetic conversions**
  (why `-1 < 0u` is false);
- use `float` and `double` knowing how many decimal digits each carries — and
  **prove** where the numbers 7 and 16 come from;
- treat `char` as a small integer encoding a character, and `bool` as the
  result of comparisons;
- explain **memory, addresses and pointers**; use `&`, `*`, `NULL` and pointer
  arithmetic, and **prove** that `a[i]` and `*(a + i)` are the same thing;
- work with **arrays** and **C strings**, explain why `strlen` is $O(n)$, and
  **prove** that building a string with repeated `strcat` is quadratic;
- recognise the memory errors — out-of-bounds access, dangling pointers,
  buffer overflows — that make C powerful and dangerous.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
The data types of C (integers, floating-point numbers, characters, booleans),
pointers, and the basic containers of C: arrays and strings.
:::

## Intuition: boxes with a size, an address and no labels

In Python a variable is a **sticky note** attached to an object that carries
its own type (@sec-variables). C is closer to the machine. A C variable *is*
a **box**: a fixed number of bytes at a fixed place in memory. The box has

- a **size**, decided by its type (4 bytes for a typical `int`);
- an **address**, the number of its first byte in memory;
- a **content**, a pattern of bits — and *no* label saying what the bits mean.

The **type** exists only in the source code: it tells the compiler how many
bytes to reserve and how to interpret the bits (as an unsigned number, a
signed number, a floating-point number, a character code…). At run time there
are only bytes. Everything in this chapter — overflow, conversions, pointers,
arrays, strings — follows from this picture.

## A first C program {#sec-first-c}

C was created by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs between 1969 and 1973 to rewrite
the Unix operating system [@ritchie1993]; its classic description is the book
by Kernighan and Ritchie, "K&R" [@kernighan1988]. C++ (@sec-ch-c-vs-cpp) is
built on it: almost every C program is also a C++ program, and the types of
this chapter are the same in both languages.

```{python}
run(r"""
/* hello.c — a first C program */
#include <stdio.h>                 /* declarations of printf, scanf, fopen, ... */

int main(void)                     /* main returns an int: the exit status */
{
    int year = 1972;               /* a variable: type, name, initial value */
    double pi = 3.14159;
    printf("C was born around %d.\n", year);
    printf("pi is about %.2f, and %d / %d = %d (integer division)\n", pi, 7, 2, 7 / 2);
    return 0;
}
""", name="hello.c")
```

Every statement ends with `;`, blocks are delimited by `{ }` (indentation is
for humans only), comments are `/* … */` or `// …`, and every variable must be
**declared with its type** before use. `printf` ("print formatted") writes its
first argument, replacing each **conversion specification** starting with `%`
by the next argument:

| Specifier | Type of the argument | Example output |
|---|---|---|
| `%d`, `%i` | `int` | `-42` |
| `%u` | `unsigned int` | `42` |
| `%ld`, `%lld` | `long`, `long long` | `9000000000` |
| `%zu` | `size_t` (sizes) | `8` |
| `%x` | `unsigned int`, in hexadecimal | `2a` |
| `%f`, `%.2f` | `double` (`float` is converted to `double`) | `3.141593`, `3.14` |
| `%e`, `%g` | `double`, scientific / shortest | `3.141593e+00`, `3.14159` |
| `%c` | a character (`int`) | `A` |
| `%s` | a string (`char *`) | `hello` |
| `%p` | a pointer (`void *`) | `0x7ffd5e8c` |

: The most common `printf` conversion specifications {#tbl-printf}

::: {.callout-warning}
## The format must match the argument
`printf` cannot check its arguments at run time: printing a `double` with
`%d` is **undefined behaviour** (@sec-ub) and prints garbage. Compile with
`-Wall`: GCC checks format strings against the arguments and warns.
:::

## Integer types {#sec-c-integers}

### Sizes and ranges

C offers integer types of several sizes, each in a **signed** and an
**unsigned** version. The standard does not fix their sizes; it fixes
**minimum ranges** and an order: `char` ≤ `short` ≤ `int` ≤ `long` ≤
`long long` [@iso9899, §5.2.4.2.1 and §6.2.5]. `sizeof` gives the size of a
type in bytes; `<limits.h>` gives the actual limits:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <limits.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    printf("%-20s %5s %22s %22s\n", "type", "bytes", "min", "max");
    printf("%-20s %5zu %22d %22d\n", "signed char", sizeof(signed char), SCHAR_MIN, SCHAR_MAX);
    printf("%-20s %5zu %22d %22d\n", "short", sizeof(short), SHRT_MIN, SHRT_MAX);
    printf("%-20s %5zu %22d %22d\n", "int", sizeof(int), INT_MIN, INT_MAX);
    printf("%-20s %5zu %22ld %22ld\n", "long", sizeof(long), LONG_MIN, LONG_MAX);
    printf("%-20s %5zu %22lld %22lld\n", "long long", sizeof(long long), LLONG_MIN, LLONG_MAX);
    printf("%-20s %5zu %22u %22u\n", "unsigned int", sizeof(unsigned), 0u, UINT_MAX);
    printf("%-20s %5zu %22u %22llu\n", "unsigned long long", sizeof(unsigned long long), 0u, ULLONG_MAX);
    return 0;
}
""", name="limits.c")
```

These are the values of 64-bit Linux (the LP64 data model of
@tbl-data-models). The pattern is no accident:

::: {#prp-int-ranges}
## Ranges of $n$-bit integers
With $n$ bits, an unsigned integer type represents exactly the integers
$0, 1, \dots, 2^n - 1$, and a signed type in two's complement exactly
$-2^{n-1}, \dots, 2^{n-1}-1$.
:::

*In one line:* $n$ bits give $2^n$ patterns; unsigned uses them all for
non-negative numbers, two's complement gives half of them to negative numbers.

This is @thm-bit-strings and @thm-twos-complement of Part I; for $n = 32$ the
signed range is $[-2\,147\,483\,648,\ 2\,147\,483\,647]$, which you can check in
the table. Since C23, two's complement is *required* for signed integers; C17
still allowed two other representations that no current machine uses.

### Fixed-width types

When the size matters — file formats, network protocols, hashing, portability
between Linux and Windows (@tbl-data-models) — use the types of
`<stdint.h>` (C99), whose names say their width: `int8_t`, `int16_t`,
`int32_t`, `int64_t` and the unsigned `uint8_t` … `uint64_t`. For sizes and
counts of objects in memory, use `size_t`, the unsigned type returned by
`sizeof` and by functions like `strlen`.

### Unsigned arithmetic wraps around {#sec-unsigned-wrap}

What is `UINT_MAX + 1`? For unsigned types the C standard gives a precise
answer: arithmetic is performed **modulo $2^n$** [@iso9899, §6.2.5]. The result
wraps around to 0, like a car's odometer:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    uint8_t  small = 250;
    uint32_t big   = 4294967295u;            /* 2^32 - 1 */
    small = small + 10;                      /* 260 mod 256 */
    big   = big + 1;                         /* 2^32 mod 2^32 */
    uint32_t x = 3000000000u, y = 2000000000u;
    printf("small = %u, big = %u\n", small, big);
    printf("x + y = %u   (5000000000 mod 2^32 = %llu)\n", x + y, 5000000000ull % 4294967296ull);
    printf("0u - 1 = %u\n", 0u - 1);         /* wraps to UINT_MAX */
    return 0;
}
""", name="wrap.c")
```

Why is this well defined and useful? Because computing modulo $2^n$ at every
step gives the same result as computing exactly and reducing at the end.

::: {#thm-mod-arith}
## Reduction modulo $m$ commutes with $+$ and $\times$
For integers $a, b$ and $m \ge 1$, writing $a \bmod m$ for the remainder of
the Euclidean division (@lem-division):
$$
(a + b) \bmod m = \big((a \bmod m) + (b \bmod m)\big) \bmod m, \qquad
(a b) \bmod m = \big((a \bmod m)(b \bmod m)\big) \bmod m .
$$
Consequently, any expression built from $+$, $-$ and $\times$ and evaluated in
`uint32_t` (resp. `uint64_t`) gives the exact mathematical value reduced
modulo $2^{32}$ (resp. $2^{64}$), whatever wrap-arounds happen along the way.
:::

*In one line:* the low $n$ bits of a sum or product depend only on the low $n$
bits of the operands, so throwing away the high bits early loses nothing that
the low bits of the final result need.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-mod-arith
Write $a = q_a m + r_a$ and $b = q_b m + r_b$ with $r_a = a \bmod m$ and
$r_b = b \bmod m$. Then $a + b = (q_a + q_b) m + (r_a + r_b)$, so $a + b$ and
$r_a + r_b$ differ by a multiple of $m$ and have the same remainder modulo $m$.
Likewise
$ab = (q_a q_b m + q_a r_b + q_b r_a)\, m + r_a r_b$, so $ab$ and $r_a r_b$
have the same remainder. Subtraction is addition of $-b$, and
$(-b) \bmod m = (m - r_b) \bmod m$, so it is covered too.

For the consequence, induct on the structure of the expression: a constant or
variable is stored reduced; if two sub-expressions evaluate to the reductions
of their exact values, the identities above show that the machine operation —
which computes the exact result of the reduced operands and reduces it —
yields the reduction of the exact value of the whole expression.
$\blacksquare$
:::

This is why hash functions and random-number generators are written with
unsigned types: their formulas are *defined* modulo $2^{32}$ or $2^{64}$, and
the hardware computes exactly that for free.

### Signed overflow is undefined behaviour {#sec-ub}

For **signed** types the standard says the opposite: if the mathematical
result does not fit, the behaviour is **undefined**.

::: {#def-ub}
## Undefined behaviour
**Undefined behaviour** (UB) is behaviour "for which this document imposes no
requirements" [@iso9899, §3.4.3]: if a program executes an operation with
undefined behaviour, the standard says nothing about what the *whole* program
does — it may crash, print garbage, or appear to work.
:::

Signed overflow, reading an uninitialised variable, dividing by zero, accessing
an array out of bounds, and dereferencing a null or dangling pointer are all
undefined. UB exists so that compilers can generate fast code on every
machine: the optimiser is allowed to **assume it never happens**. The
consequences can be startling:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <limits.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int will_not_overflow(int x) { return x + 1 > x; }   /* "obviously" true... unless x == INT_MAX */

int main(void)
{
    printf("will_not_overflow(INT_MAX) = %d\n", will_not_overflow(INT_MAX));
    return 0;
}
""", name="ub.c")
sh("gcc -std=c17 -O2 -S ub.c -o - | sed -n '/^will_not_overflow:/,/ret/p' | grep -v '\\.cfi'")
```

With two's complement wrap-around, `INT_MAX + 1` would be `INT_MIN` and the
comparison false. But the optimiser reasoned: "signed overflow cannot happen,
so `x + 1 > x` is always true", and compiled the function to `return 1`
(`movl $1, %eax`). Wang et al. found such optimisations silently removing
security checks in real systems software [@wang2013]; Lattner's essay explains
the compiler writer's side [@lattner2011]. The defence is to **test before**
computing (`if (x == INT_MAX) …`), to use unsigned types when wrap-around is
intended, and to run tests with `-fsanitize=undefined` (@sec-flags), which
reports the overflow at run time:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <limits.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int x = INT_MAX;
    int y = x + 1;                 /* signed overflow */
    printf("%d\n", y);
    return 0;
}
""", name="overflow.c", sanitize="undefined", flags=("-O0",))
```

### Mixing types: promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions {#sec-conversions}

An arithmetic operator needs operands of the **same** type. When they differ,
C converts them implicitly, following rules that every C and C++ programmer
must know [@iso9899, §6.3.1]:

1. **Integer promotion**: operands smaller than `int` (`char`, `short`,
   `uint8_t`, …) are first converted to `int`.
2. **Usual arithmetic conversions**: if one operand is floating-point, the
   other is converted to that floating type (the larger one if both are);
   otherwise, the operand of lower **rank** is converted to the type of higher
   rank (`int` < `long` < `long long`), and if a signed and an unsigned operand
   have the same rank, **the signed one is converted to unsigned**.

Rule 2's last clause causes one of C's classic traps:

::: {#exm-minus-one}
## Why `-1 < 0u` is false
In `-1 < 0u` the operands are `int` and `unsigned int`, of the same rank, so
`-1` is converted to `unsigned int`. Conversion to an unsigned type is
reduction modulo $2^{32}$: $-1 \bmod 2^{32} = 2^{32} - 1 = 4\,294\,967\,295$.
The comparison evaluated is $4\,294\,967\,295 < 0$: false. The same happens in
`for (int i = 0; i < v_size; ++i)` when `v_size` is a `size_t` and `i` becomes
negative — which is why GCC warns about signed/unsigned comparisons
(@sec-flags).
:::

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

int main(void)
{
    printf("-1 < 0u        : %d\n", -1 < 0u);
    printf("(unsigned)-1   : %u\n", (unsigned)-1);
    printf("7 / 2 = %d, 7 / 2.0 = %g, (double)7 / 2 = %g\n", 7 / 2, 7 / 2.0, (double)7 / 2);
    printf("-7 / 2 = %d, -7 %% 2 = %d   (C truncates toward zero)\n", -7 / 2, -7 % 2);
    if (strlen("abc") - 4 > 0)                          /* size_t arithmetic: 3 - 4 wraps! */
        printf("strlen(\"abc\") - 4 > 0 is true: %zu\n", strlen("abc") - 4);
    return 0;
}
""", name="conversions.c", flags=("-O2",))
```

Note also that **integer division truncates toward zero** in C (`-7 / 2` is
`-3`), unlike Python's `//`, which floors (`-7 // 2` is `-4`, @eq-floor-div).
An explicit **cast** `(double)x` converts a value on purpose.

## The bits behind a type {.deep}

The same 8, 16 or 32 bits mean different numbers depending on the type through
which they are read. Choose a width and a bit pattern (as an unsigned value)
and compare the unsigned and two's-complement readings (@eq-twos):

::: {.widget}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bitsN = Inputs.radio([8, 16, 32], {value: 8, label: "width n (bits)"})
viewof bitsU = Inputs.range([0, 2 ** bitsN - 1], {step: 1, value: Math.min(200, 2 ** bitsN - 1), label: "unsigned value"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bitsRow = {
  const n = bitsN, u = Math.min(bitsU, 2 ** n - 1);
  const pattern = u.toString(2).padStart(n, "0").replace(/(.{4})(?=.)/g, "$1 ");
  const signed = u >= 2 ** (n - 1) ? u - 2 ** n : u;
  return [{"bit pattern": pattern, "as unsigned": u, "as signed (two's complement)": signed,
           "hexadecimal": "0x" + u.toString(16).padStart(n / 4, "0")}];
}
Inputs.table(bitsRow, {layout: "auto"})
```
:::

Try $n = 8$ with values 127, 128 and 255: the signed reading jumps from $127$ to
$-128$ and reaches $-1$ — wrap-around and the conversion of
@exm-minus-one, seen from the bits.



## Floating-point types {#sec-c-floats}

C has three floating-point types: `float`, `double` and `long double`. On all
common platforms `float` and `double` are the IEEE 754 **binary32** and
**binary64** formats [@ieee754]; Python's `float` *is* a C `double`
(@sec-floats). Their significands have $p = 24$ and $p = 53$ bits respectively.
How many decimal digits is that?

::: {#prp-decimal-digits}
## Decimal precision of a binary format
In a binary floating-point format with a $p$-bit significand, the gap between
a normal number $x$ and the next one is between $2^{-p}|x|$ and
$2^{1-p}|x|$. The format therefore carries about $p \log_{10} 2$ significant
decimal digits: $7.22$ for `float` and $15.95$ for `double`.
:::

*In one line:* each significand bit is worth $\log_{10} 2 \approx 0.301$
decimal digits, so 24 bits ≈ 7 digits and 53 bits ≈ 16 digits.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-decimal-digits
Let $2^E \le |x| < 2^{E+1}$. As in the proof of @thm-rounding-error, the
numbers of the format in $[2^E, 2^{E+1}]$ are equally spaced with gap
$g = 2^{E - (p-1)} = 2^{E+1-p}$. Dividing by $|x|$ and using
$2^E \le |x| < 2^{E+1}$ gives $2^{-p} < g/|x| \le 2^{1-p}$. A relative
resolution of $2^{-p}$ corresponds to $q$ decimal digits when $10^{-q} = 2^{-p}$,
i.e. $q = p \log_{10} 2$; with $\log_{10} 2 \approx 0.30103$ this is
$24 \times 0.30103 = 7.22$ and $53 \times 0.30103 = 15.95$. $\blacksquare$
:::

The C standard publishes two related constants, derived by Matula
[@matula1968]: `FLT_DIG` / `DBL_DIG`, the number of decimal digits that
survive a decimal → binary → decimal round trip,
$\lfloor (p-1)\log_{10} 2 \rfloor$ (6 and 15); and `FLT_DECIMAL_DIG` /
`DBL_DECIMAL_DIG`, the digits needed to print a binary number so that reading
it back gives the same bits, $\lceil 1 + p \log_{10} 2 \rceil$ (9 and 17). The
practical lesson: use **`double`** unless memory is tight (as in GPU tensors,
where `float` and even 16-bit formats are common); `float` runs out of digits
quickly.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <float.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    printf("FLT_DIG = %d, DBL_DIG = %d, FLT_DECIMAL_DIG = %d, DBL_DECIMAL_DIG = %d\n",
           FLT_DIG, DBL_DIG, FLT_DECIMAL_DIG, DBL_DECIMAL_DIG);
    float f = 0.1f;
    double d = 0.1;
    printf("0.1 as float : %.20f\n0.1 as double: %.20f\n", f, d);

    float fsum = 0.0f;
    double dsum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 10000000; ++i) {     /* add 0.1 ten million times */
        fsum += 0.1f;
        dsum += 0.1;
    }
    printf("sum in float : %.6f\nsum in double: %.6f   (exact: 1000000)\n", fsum, dsum);
    printf("16777216.0f + 1.0f = %.1f\n", 16777216.0f + 1.0f);   /* 2^24 + 1 is not a float */
    return 0;
}
""", name="floats.c", flags=("-O2",))
```

The `float` sum is off by almost 9%. Each addition is rounded to a multiple of
the gap between consecutive floats near the running total (@prp-decimal-digits):
between $2^{18}$ and $2^{19}$ the gap is $1/32$ and $0.1$ is effectively added
as $3/32 = 0.09375$; between $2^{19}$ and $2^{20}$ the gap is $1/16$ and $0.1$
becomes $2/16 = 0.125$. The errors no longer cancel. From
$2^{24} \approx 1.7\times 10^7$ on, the gap is 2 and even adding 1 has no
effect, as the last line shows. The rules
of @sec-floats — never compare floats for exact equality, beware of
accumulated error — apply unchanged in C.

## Characters: `char` {#sec-c-char}

A `char` is a **one-byte integer**. What makes it a "character" is only the
convention that its value is a code in a character set — on every current
system an extension of **ASCII**, the 1963 American standard that assigns codes
0–127 to letters, digits, punctuation and control characters [@rfc20]. A
character literal like `'A'` is just a way of writing the integer 65:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <ctype.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    char c = 'A';
    printf("'%c' has code %d; next is '%c'\n", c, c, c + 1);
    printf("'7' - '0' = %d   (digit character -> number)\n", '7' - '0');
    printf("toupper('q') = '%c', isdigit('5') = %d, isalpha('5') = %d\n",
           toupper('q'), isdigit('5') != 0, isalpha('5') != 0);
    printf("newline = %d, tab = %d, NUL = %d\n", '\n', '\t', '\0');
    return 0;
}
""", name="chars.c")
```

Two facts matter in practice:

- `'0'`, `'1'`, …, `'9'` have **consecutive** codes (the standard guarantees
  it), so `c - '0'` converts a digit character to its value — the core of
  every hand-written number parser;
- whether plain `char` is signed or unsigned is **implementation-defined**
  (signed on x86, unsigned on ARM Linux). Bytes above 127, such as the UTF-8
  encoding of `è` (@sec-utf8), may thus become negative numbers. Pass
  characters to the `<ctype.h>` functions as `unsigned char`.

A C `char` is a **byte**, not a Unicode character: `"è"` is a string of *two*
`char`s in UTF-8. C and C++ programs that handle international text either
treat strings as opaque UTF-8 bytes (as the project does) or use a dedicated
library.

## Booleans {#sec-c-bool}

Early C had no Boolean type: comparisons and logical operators produce the
`int` values `1` (true) and `0` (false), and in a condition **any non-zero
scalar is true** — like Python's truthiness, but only for numbers and
pointers (@sec-truthiness). C99 added the type `_Bool` and the header
`<stdbool.h>` with the names `bool`, `true`, `false`; since C23 they are
keywords, as they always were in C++.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    bool ok = (3 < 5);
    printf("3 < 5 is %d, 3 > 5 is %d, sizeof(bool) = %zu\n", ok, 3 > 5, sizeof(bool));
    bool b = 42;                        /* conversion to bool: any non-zero value -> 1 */
    printf("(bool)42 = %d\n", b);
    if (-3) printf("-3 counts as true in a condition\n");
    return 0;
}
""", name="bools.c")
```

## Memory, addresses and pointers {#sec-pointers}

### The model

To C, memory is a huge **array of bytes**, numbered from 0: the number of a
byte is its **address** (@sec-von-neumann). A variable of type `T` occupies
`sizeof(T)` consecutive bytes; its address is the address of the first one.

::: {#def-pointer}
## Pointer
A **pointer** to `T` (type `T *`) is a variable whose value is the address of
an object of type `T`. The operator `&` gives the address of a variable
(`&x`); the operator `*` **dereferences** a pointer, i.e. denotes the object it
points to (`*p`). The special value `NULL` (C23 and C++: `nullptr`) points to
no object.
:::

*In one line:* a pointer is an address with a type attached, so the compiler
knows what lives at that address.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int x = 10;
    int *p = &x;                       /* p holds the address of x */
    printf("x = %d, *p = %d\n", x, *p);
    *p = 20;                           /* write THROUGH the pointer: changes x */
    printf("after *p = 20, x = %d\n", x);
    printf("sizeof(int) = %zu, sizeof(int *) = %zu, sizeof(double *) = %zu\n",
           sizeof(int), sizeof(int *), sizeof(double *));
    int *q = NULL;
    if (q == NULL) printf("q points nowhere; dereferencing it would be undefined behaviour\n");
    return 0;
}
""", name="pointers.c")
```

All pointers are 8 bytes on a 64-bit machine, whatever they point to: an
address is an address. The type `int *` matters for what `*p` *means* (read 4
bytes as an `int`) and for pointer arithmetic.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-cap: "A pointer p holding the address of x. Addresses are illustrative; each int occupies 4 bytes."
flowchart LR
    subgraph memory["memory (addresses grow →)"]
      direction LR
      X["x : int<br/>address 1000<br/>value 20"]
      P["p : int*<br/>address 1008<br/>value 1000"]
    end
    P -- "*p" --> X
```

Why would we want pointers? Three reasons, which we will meet in turn:

1. to let a function **modify** the caller's variables (C passes arguments by
   value, @sec-ch-c-tools);
2. to refer to **large objects** without copying them;
3. to manage memory whose size is known only **at run time** (@sec-malloc) and
   to build linked data structures.

### Pointer arithmetic

If `p` points to an element of an array, `p + 1` points to the **next
element**, not to the next byte:

::: {#def-pointer-arith}
## Pointer arithmetic
For a pointer `p` of type `T *` and an integer `i`, `p + i` is the pointer of
type `T *` whose address is $\text{address}(p) + i \cdot \texttt{sizeof(T)}$.
It is defined only if both `p` and `p + i` point into the same array (or one
past its last element). The difference `q - p` of two pointers into the same
array is the number of elements between them.
:::

::: {#prp-subscript}
## Subscripting is pointer arithmetic
For an array or pointer `a` and an integer `i`, the expression `a[i]` is
*defined* by the standard as `*(a + i)` [@iso9899, §6.5.2.1]. Consequently
`a[i]`, `*(a + i)`, `*(i + a)` and even `i[a]` all denote the same object.
:::

*In one line:* indexing is "start at the beginning, skip $i$ elements, look
there" — exactly the address formula $\text{base} + i\cdot s$ of
@sec-indexing.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-subscript
`a[i]` ≡ `*(a + i)` by definition. Addition of a pointer and an integer is
commutative by @def-pointer-arith (the address computed for `i + a` is the
same, $\text{address}(a) + i\cdot\texttt{sizeof(T)}$), so `*(a + i)` ≡
`*(i + a)`, which by the same definition of subscripting is `i[a]`.
$\blacksquare$
:::

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
    int *p = a;                                 /* the array "decays" to &a[0] */
    printf("a[2] = %d, *(a + 2) = %d, 2[a] = %d, *(p + 2) = %d\n", a[2], *(a + 2), 2[a], *(p + 2));
    printf("byte distance between &a[3] and &a[0]: %td\n", (char *)&a[3] - (char *)&a[0]);
    printf("element distance (&a[3] - &a[0]): %td\n", &a[3] - &a[0]);
    for (int *q = a; q < a + 5; ++q)            /* walk the array with a pointer */
        printf("%d ", *q);
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
""", name="arith.c")
```

(`2[a]` is legal and means `a[2]`; it is shown only to make the proposition
concrete — never write it.)

## Arrays {#sec-c-arrays}

An **array** `T a[N]` is `N` objects of type `T` stored **contiguously**. It
is the only built-in container of C, and it is what Python's list is built on
(@sec-dynamic-arrays). Its properties follow from the model:

- **fixed size**: `N` must be known when the array is created and never
  changes;
- **$O(1)$ access** to any element, by @def-pointer-arith;
- **no bounds checking**: `a[N]` or `a[-1]` compile and silently read or write
  someone else's memory — undefined behaviour (sanitizers catch it,
  @sec-flags);
- **decay**: in most expressions the name of an array is converted to a pointer
  to its first element; in particular an array **passed to a function arrives
  as a pointer**, and the function no longer knows its length.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>

double average(const double *values, size_t n)   /* the length must travel separately */
{
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        sum += values[i];
    return n ? sum / n : 0.0;
}

int main(void)
{
    double temps[] = {21.5, 23.0, 19.5, 22.0};               /* size deduced: 4 */
    size_t n = sizeof temps / sizeof temps[0];               /* bytes of the array / bytes of one element */
    printf("n = %zu, average = %.2f\n", n, average(temps, n));

    int grid[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};                 /* 2 rows of 3: stored row after row */
    printf("grid[1][2] = %d, sizeof grid = %zu bytes\n", grid[1][2], sizeof grid);
    return 0;
}
""", name="arrays.c")
```

The idiom `sizeof a / sizeof a[0]` works **only** where `a` is a true array;
inside `average`, `values` is a pointer and `sizeof values` would be 8. A
two-dimensional array is stored **row by row** (row-major order), so element
`[i][j]` of a `R × C` array is at offset $iC + j$ — the layout NumPy calls
C order.

## Strings {#sec-c-strings}

C has no string type. A **C string** is an array of `char` that contains the
characters followed by a terminating **null character** `'\0'` (value 0). The
literal `"cat"` is an array of **four** `char`s: `'c' 'a' 't' '\0'`.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

int main(void)
{
    char word[] = "cat";                         /* {'c','a','t','\0'} */
    printf("sizeof word = %zu, strlen(word) = %zu\n", sizeof word, strlen(word));
    for (size_t i = 0; i <= strlen(word); ++i)
        printf("word[%zu] = %3d '%c'\n", i, word[i], word[i] ? word[i] : '0');

    char buffer[32];
    snprintf(buffer, sizeof buffer, "%s has %zu letters", word, strlen(word));  /* bounded write */
    printf("%s\n", buffer);
    printf("strcmp(\"apple\", \"banana\") = %d (negative: comes first)\n",
           strcmp("apple", "banana") < 0 ? -1 : 1);
    return 0;
}
""", name="strings.c")
```

| Function (`<string.h>`, `<stdio.h>`) | Does | Watch out |
|---|---|---|
| `strlen(s)` | number of characters before `'\0'` | $O(n)$: it scans |
| `strcmp(a, b)` | $<0$, $0$, $>0$: lexicographic order of byte values (@sec-sorting) | `a == b` compares **addresses**, not contents |
| `strcpy(dst, src)` | copies `src` into `dst` | no size check: overflows `dst` |
| `strcat(dst, src)` | appends `src` at the end of `dst` | no size check; rescans `dst` |
| `snprintf(dst, n, fmt, …)` | formatted write of at most `n - 1` chars + `'\0'` | the safe default for building strings |
| `strchr(s, c)`, `strstr(s, t)` | find a character / a substring | return a pointer or `NULL` |

: Common C string functions {#tbl-c-strings}

### The cost of not storing the length

Because a C string does not store its length, `strlen` must **walk** until the
`'\0'`: $\Theta(n)$ for a string of length $n$, where Python's `len` is $O(1)$.
The cost compounds in loops. Joel Spolsky called the resulting pattern
**Shlemiel the painter's algorithm**, after a painter who keeps walking back to
the paint can at the start of the road [@spolsky2001]:

::: {#prp-schlemiel}
## Repeated `strcat` is quadratic
Appending $k$ pieces of length $L$ each to an initially empty string with
`strcat` reads $\Theta(k^2 L)$ characters. Keeping a pointer to the current end
and copying each piece there reads $\Theta(kL)$ characters.
:::

*In one line:* each `strcat` first walks over everything appended so far, and
"everything so far" grows linearly.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-schlemiel
Before the $j$-th append ($j = 1, \dots, k$) the string has length $(j-1)L$.
`strcat` scans those $(j-1)L$ characters to find the end, then copies $L$
characters. The total is
$$
\sum_{j=1}^{k} \big((j-1)L + L\big) = L \sum_{j=1}^{k} j = L\,\frac{k(k+1)}{2} = \Theta(k^2 L),
$$
using Gauss's formula (@eq-gauss). With an end pointer, the scan disappears and
each append costs $L$: total $kL$. $\blacksquare$
:::

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>

enum { PIECES = 40000, PIECE_LEN = 5 };
static char buffer[PIECES * PIECE_LEN + 1];

int main(void)
{
    clock_t t0 = clock();
    buffer[0] = '\0';
    for (int i = 0; i < PIECES; ++i)
        strcat(buffer, "abcde");                        /* rescans from the start every time */
    double t_strcat = (double)(clock() - t0) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC;

    t0 = clock();
    char *end = buffer;
    for (int i = 0; i < PIECES; ++i) {
        memcpy(end, "abcde", PIECE_LEN);                /* write at the known end */
        end += PIECE_LEN;
    }
    *end = '\0';
    double t_end = (double)(clock() - t0) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC;

    printf("length %zu: strcat %.3f s, end pointer %.6f s\n", strlen(buffer), t_strcat, t_end);
    return 0;
}
""", name="schlemiel.c", flags=("-O2",))
```

C++'s `std::string` (@sec-ch-c-vs-cpp) stores the length and the capacity,
like a dynamic array, so its `size()` is $O(1)$ and `+=` is $O(1)$ amortised
per character (@thm-amortized-append).

### Buffer overflows

`strcpy`, `strcat`, `sprintf` and the input function `gets` write as many
bytes as the source provides, regardless of the size of the destination. A
longer input overwrites whatever lies next in memory — other variables, or the
saved return address of the function, which an attacker can redirect to code of
their choosing. The Morris worm of 1988, one of the first Internet worms,
spread, among other ways, by overflowing a buffer filled by `gets` in the
`fingerd` server [@spafford1989]. `gets` was removed from the language in C11. Decades
later, memory-safety errors — buffer overflows, use after free, and their
relatives — were still the root cause of about 70% of the vulnerabilities
Microsoft fixed each year [@miller2019]. The rules:

- always pass the **size** of the destination (`snprintf`, `fgets`,
  `strncat` with care), and check return values;
- prefer data structures that know their size: in C++, `std::string` and
  `std::vector` (@sec-ch-c-vs-cpp);
- test with **AddressSanitizer**.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

int main(void)
{
    char name[8];
    const char *input = "Bartholomew";              /* 11 characters + '\0' = 12 bytes */
    strcpy(name, input);                            /* writes 12 bytes into 8 */
    printf("%s\n", name);
    return 0;
}
""", name="overflow_str.c", sanitize="address", flags=("-O0", "-Wall"), filter_lines=sanitizer_summary)
```

Here GCC already warns at compile time, because both sizes are constants; when
the string comes from the user or a file, only a run-time check — or a correct
program — can help. The sanitizer stops the program at the faulty `strcpy`
(frame `#1 … in main overflow_str.c:8`).

## Arrays of run-time size: `malloc` and `free` {#sec-malloc}

Arrays declared in a function live on the **stack** and disappear when the
function returns; their size must be known in advance. For data whose size is
known only at run time — the number of records in a file — C programs ask the
system for memory on the **heap**: `malloc(n)` returns a pointer to `n` fresh
bytes (or `NULL` if none are available), `realloc` resizes a block (possibly
moving it), and `free` gives the memory back.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main(void)
{
    size_t n = 0, capacity = 2;
    int *v = malloc(capacity * sizeof *v);           /* room for 2 ints */
    if (v == NULL) return 1;
    for (int x = 1; x <= 10; ++x) {
        if (n == capacity) {                         /* full: double the capacity */
            capacity *= 2;
            int *bigger = realloc(v, capacity * sizeof *v);
            if (bigger == NULL) { free(v); return 1; }
            v = bigger;
            printf("grew to capacity %zu\n", capacity);
        }
        v[n++] = x * x;
    }
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) printf("%d ", v[i]);
    printf("\n");
    free(v);                                         /* every malloc needs exactly one free */
    return 0;
}
""", name="dynarray.c")
```

This is a **dynamic array** built by hand, with the doubling strategy whose
$O(1)$ amortised cost we proved in @thm-amortized-append. The burden is on
the programmer: forgetting `free` **leaks** memory; using `v` after `free`
(a **dangling pointer**) or freeing twice is undefined behaviour. C++ removes
most of this burden with constructors, destructors and `std::vector`
(@sec-ch-c-vs-cpp); the CRM never calls `malloc`.

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** The CRM (@sec-ch-project-crm) is written in C++ and uses
`std::string` and the standard containers rather than C arrays and C strings,
for exactly the reasons of @sec-c-strings: they know their size and grow on
demand. This chapter still shapes the design: customer and interaction
**identifiers** are unsigned integers of a fixed width (`std::uint32_t`,
@sec-c-integers), dates are validated objects written in the ISO form
`YYYY-MM-DD`, which sorts correctly even as text, and premium amounts are kept as **integer cents** (a `std::int64_t`)
rather than `double`, so that 0.10 + 0.20 is exactly 0.30 (@sec-c-floats).
Parsing user input into these types safely is the subject of @sec-ch-c-tools.
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Assuming sizes**: `int` is not necessarily 32 bits, `long` is 32 bits on
  Windows. Use `<stdint.h>` when it matters, `size_t` for sizes.
- **Signed overflow**: undefined, not "wrap-around". Check before computing.
- **Mixing signed and unsigned**: `-1 < 0u` is false; `strlen(s) - 1` with an
  empty string is a huge number.
- **Integer division**: `7 / 2` is `3`; cast first (`(double)7 / 2`).
- **`float` for money or large sums**: use `double`, or integers in cents.
- **Uninitialised variables and pointers**: their value is indeterminate.
- **Out-of-bounds access**: not checked; undefined behaviour.
- **`sizeof` on an array parameter**: it is a pointer; pass the length.
- **`==` on strings** compares addresses: use `strcmp`.
- **Forgetting the `'\0'`**: a string of $n$ characters needs $n + 1$ bytes.
- **Unbounded string functions** (`strcpy`, `strcat`, `sprintf`, `gets`):
  use bounded ones and check sizes.
- **Leaks, double `free`, use after `free`.**
:::

## Summary

- A C variable is a box of `sizeof(T)` bytes at an address; types exist at
  compile time and decide size and interpretation.
- Integer types have minimum ranges; with $n$ bits, unsigned covers
  $[0, 2^n-1]$ and two's complement $[-2^{n-1}, 2^{n-1}-1]$. **Unsigned
  arithmetic is modulo $2^n$** (@thm-mod-arith); **signed overflow is undefined
  behaviour**, and optimisers exploit it.
- Mixed operands undergo **promotions** and the **usual arithmetic
  conversions**; signed meets unsigned → unsigned.
- `float` ≈ 7 and `double` ≈ 16 significant digits (@prp-decimal-digits);
  prefer `double`.
- `char` is a one-byte integer holding a character code; `bool` (C99/C23) holds
  0 or 1; any non-zero scalar is true.
- A **pointer** holds an address; `&` takes it, `*` follows it; `p + i` moves
  by $i$ elements, and `a[i]` *is* `*(a + i)` (@prp-subscript).
- **Arrays** are fixed-size, contiguous, unchecked, and decay to pointers.
  **C strings** are `'\0'`-terminated arrays: `strlen` is $O(n)$ and repeated
  `strcat` is quadratic (@prp-schlemiel); unbounded writes cause buffer
  overflows.
- `malloc`/`realloc`/`free` manage heap memory by hand.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-cpp3-ranges}
For a 16-bit `short`, give `SHRT_MIN` and `SHRT_MAX`. What is the value of
`(unsigned short)-2`? And of `(short)40000`? (Converting an out-of-range value
to a signed type is implementation-defined in C; C++20 defines it as reduction
modulo $2^n$, which is also what GCC does in C.)
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$[-2^{15}, 2^{15}-1] = [-32\,768, 32\,767]$. `(unsigned short)-2` is
$-2 \bmod 2^{16} = 65\,534$. `(short)40000`: $40\,000 \bmod 2^{16} = 40\,000$,
which lies in the upper half of the 16-bit patterns, so the two's-complement
reading is $40\,000 - 65\,536 = -25\,536$.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp3-hash}
The FNV-1a hash of a byte string is computed as: `h = 2166136261`; for each
byte `b`: `h = (h ^ b) * 16777619`, all in `uint32_t`. Write it in C and use
@thm-mod-arith to explain why the result is the same on every platform even
though the multiplication overflows at almost every step.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```c
#include <stdint.h>
uint32_t fnv1a(const unsigned char *s, size_t n) {
    uint32_t h = 2166136261u;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        h ^= s[i];
        h *= 16777619u;          /* wraps modulo 2^32: well defined for unsigned */
    }
    return h;
}
```
`uint32_t` arithmetic is defined as arithmetic modulo $2^{32}$; by
@thm-mod-arith the result equals the exact value of the formula reduced modulo
$2^{32}$, which does not depend on the machine. With a signed `int32_t`, the
overflow would be undefined behaviour.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp3-predict}
Predict the output, then check by compiling with warnings:
```c
unsigned u = 3; int i = -5;
printf("%d\n", u + i > 0);
printf("%d\n", -7 / 2 * 2 + -7 % 2);
char s[] = "hello";
printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof s, strlen(s));
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
`u + i`: `i` is converted to `unsigned` ($2^{32}-5$), the sum is
$2^{32} - 2$ modulo $2^{32}$, i.e. 4 294 967 294, which is $> 0$: prints `1`.
`-7 / 2 * 2 + -7 % 2` $= (-3)\cdot 2 + (-1) = -7$: C guarantees
`(a/b)*b + a%b == a`. `sizeof s` is 6 (five letters and `'\0'`), `strlen(s)`
is 5.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp3-pointers}
Write a function `void minmax(const int *a, size_t n, int *min, int *max)` that
stores the minimum and the maximum of a non-empty array in the variables
pointed to by `min` and `max`. Why does it need pointers for the results?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```c
void minmax(const int *a, size_t n, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = *max = a[0];
    for (size_t i = 1; i < n; ++i) {
        if (a[i] < *min) *min = a[i];
        if (a[i] > *max) *max = a[i];
    }
}
/* usage: int lo, hi; minmax(v, 5, &lo, &hi); */
```
C passes arguments by value: the function receives copies. To deliver two
results to the caller's variables it receives their **addresses** and writes
through them. (C++ references make this more convenient, @sec-ch-c-vs-cpp.)
:::

::: {#exr-cpp3-digits}
Using @prp-decimal-digits, how many significant decimal digits does the IEEE
754 binary16 ("half precision", $p = 11$) format carry? And bfloat16, used to
train neural networks ($p = 8$)? What does this suggest about accumulating
sums in those formats?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$11 \log_{10}2 \approx 3.3$ and $8 \log_{10} 2 \approx 2.4$ digits. With so few
digits, adding a small number to a large running sum loses it entirely (as in
the `float` experiment, but much sooner): this is why mixed-precision training
keeps accumulators and master weights in `float` (binary32).
:::

  introduction to C.
- @iso9899 — the C standard (the free draft N3220 is almost identical to
  C23): §5.2.4.2 (limits), §6.2.5 (types), §6.3 (conversions), §6.5.2.1
  (subscripting).
- @ritchie1993 — Ritchie's own history of how C's types and pointers came
  about.
- @bryant2016, ch. 2 (representing and manipulating information: integers and
  floating point, at the bit level) and ch. 3 (how arrays and pointers become
  machine code).
- @wang2013 and @lattner2011 — undefined behaviour seen by systems researchers
  and by a compiler writer.
- @seacord2013 — secure programming in C and C++, ch. 2 on strings and buffer
